name: Justin Martyr

seo.title: St Justin Martyr: philosopher, apologist, quotes and feast day
seo.description: Who Justin Martyr was, in plain words: the philosopher who found Christ, his letter to the emperor, his trial in Rome, and his words with the chapter.

band.lede: A philosopher who became a Christian, defended the faith to the emperor, and was beheaded for it.

picture.alt: A fresco of Justin as a dark-haired, bearded man with a gold halo, in a red tunic and a pale cloak, holding a small cross and a closed book, with his name in Greek beside him
picture.credit: Saint Justin the Philosopher, fresco by Theophanes the Cretan and his son Symeon, about 1546. Stavronikita Monastery, Mount Athos. Public domain.
picture.creator: Theophanes the Cretan and his son Symeon

card.line: A philosopher who became a Christian, defended the faith to the emperor, and was beheaded for it.

who: Justin was a philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian in the second century. He kept wearing his philosopher's cloak and taught in Rome. He wrote to the emperor to defend Christians, and described Christian worship in rare detail. About 165 he was beheaded in Rome with six companions.

numbers.src: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapters 3 to 5

lines: All from one copy, finished in 1364

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 100. Some say as late as 114. At Flavia Neapolis in Palestine, near ancient Shechem. Today it is **Nablus**.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In a pagan family. His grandfather's name is Greek, his father's and his own Latin. He calls himself uncircumcised, and the Samaritans his people.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: About 165, in **Rome**. He was scourged and beheaded with six companions, on the sentence of Rusticus, prefect of the city.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: The record of his trial does not say. Some believers took the bodies in secret and laid them “in a suitable place”. The OCA says his relics rest in Rome.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Justin the Philosopher**, in the Orthodox Church. In Greek he is also **the Apologist**. “Martyr” is a title, not a surname.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too, on the same day.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: **Philosophers**, in Catholic devotion. The OCA says people ask his help with their studies.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In Eastern icons, such as the fresco at the top of this page, a dark-haired, bearded man in a cloak, with a martyr's small cross and a book. The fresco labels him “the Philosopher”. A Western print of 1584 imagines him as an old man with a long beard.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: The **First Apology**, the **Second Apology** and the **Dialogue with Trypho**. Eusebius lists more books, now lost. Several works printed under his name are not his.

portrait.alt: An engraved half-length portrait of Justin as an old man with a long curly beard and a heavy cloak, both hands raised as if speaking
portrait.credit: Saint Justin Martyr, an imagined likeness engraved for André Thevet, Les vrais pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres, 1584. Public domain.
portrait.caption: An imagined likeness, engraved for André Thevet's book of portraits of famous men, 1584. Public domain.

west.text: The **Catholic** feast from Pope Leo XIII until 1969. The **1916 Roman Martyrology** tells of his death the day before, on 13 April.
**Catholic** memorial since 1969. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: **OCA** and the **Greek** churches. The **Russian Church** keeps it on the old calendar, which is 14 June on today's calendar.

feasts.note: East and West now keep the same day. Rome kept 14 April from 1882. Its new calendar of 1969 moved him to 1 June. The reason it gives: 14 April often fell among the Easter feasts, and the Byzantine churches had kept 1 June since at least the 9th century. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later.

traits.title: a restless seeker
traits.text: A famous Pythagorean told him to learn music, astronomy and geometry first. Justin could not face the wait. “Accordingly I took it rather impatiently,” he admits. “I was not able to endure longer procrastination.”

traits.title: joked, and parted friends
traits.text: When Trypho stopped him to talk, Justin answered with a line of Homer. He says he “replied to him in jest”. After two days of hard argument they parted as friends, and Justin prayed for them as they went.

traits.title: no double talk
traits.text: Trypho asked if he truly believed what he had said, or only said it to win. “I am not so miserable a fellow, Trypho, as to say one thing and think another.” He told the emperor that Christians could deny the name and walk free, “but we would not live by telling a lie”.

cite.text: Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 80; First Apology, chapter 8

traits.title: took on all comers
traits.text: He questioned the Cynic Crescens, and “found most convincingly that he, in truth, knows nothing.” He offered to do it again in front of the emperor. When Trypho's friends laughed at him, he got up to leave, and Trypho caught hold of his garment.

cite.text: Second Apology, chapter 3; Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 9

traits.title: loved a pun
traits.text: Christians were punished for the name alone. In Greek, Christ's name sounds like the word for good. So, Justin says, judged by the name, “we are most excellent people.” He called Crescens “that lover of bravado and boasting”, words that sound in Greek like “philosopher”. His translators point out both puns.

cite.text: First Apology, chapter 4; Second Apology, chapter 3

said.lede: Nearly everything about his life comes from his own books and the short record of his trial. His pupil Tatian left a line about him. Later writers who read him left more.

quotes.q: And the most admirable Justin has rightly denounced them as robbers.
quotes.who: Tatian, his pupil, on the demons

cite.text: Tatian, Address to the Greeks, chapter 18

quotes.who: Tertullian, a generation later. He names Justin first among those who had already answered the heretics.

quotes.q: Justin of Neapolis, a man not far removed either from the times or from the virtues of the apostles

cite.text: Methodius, Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 3

quotes.q: But Justin was especially prominent in those days. In the guise of a philosopher he preached the divine word, and contended for the faith in his writings.

moments.title: Shopping for a philosophy
moments.text: He went looking for God in the schools. A Stoic taught him nothing about God. A Peripatetic asked for his fee after a few days, so Justin decided he was no philosopher at all. A proud Pythagorean sent him away for not knowing music, astronomy and geometry. The Platonists thrilled him. “Such was my stupidity,” he says, “I expected forthwith to look upon God.” The *Catholic Encyclopedia* warns that the story is shaped to make a point, and “cannot be taken too literally”.

moments.title: The old man
moments.text: He liked to walk alone near the sea, to think. One day an old man followed him there. He said he had come looking for some of his household, who had gone away. Then he took Justin's Platonism apart, question by question, and sent him to the prophets. “I have not seen him since,” Justin writes. While he was still a Platonist, he had seen Christians face death without fear. He saw that they could not be living in wickedness.

cite.text: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 3 to 8; Second Apology, chapter 12

moments.title: Two days with Trypho
moments.text: One morning a Jew named Trypho, who had fled the war in Judea, greeted him in a colonnade because of his philosopher's cloak. When Trypho's friends jeered, Justin got up to go, but Trypho caught hold of his garment. They argued over the Scriptures for two days. At the end Trypho asked him to “remember us as friends when you are gone”.

cite.text: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 1, 9 and 142; Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 18

moments.title: A teacher in Rome
moments.text: He lived in Rome twice. He lodged “above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath”. Anyone who wished could come to him there, and he told them “the doctrines of truth”. One who heard him was Tatian.

cite.text: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapter 2; Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 1, chapter 28

moments.title: A letter to the emperor
moments.text: He wrote to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons, for “those of all nations who are unjustly hated and wantonly abused, myself being one of them.” He asked that Christians be judged by what they did, not by their name. He also told what Christians did at baptism and on Sunday. To leave it out, he says, would seem unfair.

moments.title: He saw it coming
moments.text: The prefect Urbicus put a Christian teacher, Ptolemaeus, to death for the name alone. A man named Lucius protested, and was led away too. Then a third man. Justin wrote again, this time to the Romans. He expected to be plotted against, perhaps by his rival, the Cynic Crescens: “I too, therefore, expect to be plotted against and fixed to the stake”.

cite.text: Second Apology, chapters 1 to 3; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910

words.note: Three of his books survive, and the record of his trial keeps his last answers. The lines are from the 1885 translation by Marcus Dods and George Reith.

feature.q: You can kill, but not hurt us.
feature.ctx: From the opening of the *First Apology*, to Antoninus Pius and his sons. No evil can be done to Christians, he says, unless they are proved to be evildoers. The thought goes back to Socrates at his own trial. In Greek, {el|ὑμεῖς δ᾽ ἀποκτεῖναι μὲν δύνασθε, βλάψαι δ᾽ οὔ.}

quotes.q: But straightway a flame was kindled in my soul; and a love of the prophets, and of those men who are friends of Christ, possessed me; and whilst revolving his words in my mind, I found this philosophy alone to be safe and profitable.
quotes.who: How he became a Christian, after the old man by the sea left him.

quotes.q: Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.
quotes.who: On the truth in Plato, the Stoics and the poets. Each spoke well, he says, in proportion to his share of the Word.

quotes.q: Those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them.
quotes.who: On good people who lived before Christ.

quotes.q: We who valued above all things the acquisition of wealth and possessions, now bring what we have into a common stock, and communicate to every one in need; we who hated and destroyed one another, and on account of their different manners would not live with men of a different tribe, now, since the coming of Christ, live familiarly with them, and pray for our enemies.
quotes.who: What becoming a Christian changed, in his words to the emperor.

quotes.q: Brief and concise utterances fell from Him, for He was no sophist, but His word was the power of God.

myths.claim: “What the soul is in the body, that are Christians in the world.”
myths.truth: Not his. It is from the Letter to Diognetus, chapter 6, by an unknown writer. After it was first printed in 1592 it was long credited to Justin. Its editors in the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* say its tone “points to some other writer than Justin.”

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, note on the Letter to Diognetus

myths.claim: “To yield and give way to our passions is the lowest slavery, even as to rule over them is the only liberty.”
myths.truth: Not in his three surviving works. It comes from a medieval book of sayings, the Melissa of Antonius, which credits it to Justin. The *Ante-Nicene Fathers* prints it among fragments whose authorship is disputed. Goodreads wrongly places it in his work on the resurrection.

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, Other Fragments, fragment 18

myths.claim: “Plain singing is not childish, but only the singing with lifeless organs, with dancing, and cymbals.”
myths.truth: The line is from the Answers to the Orthodox, question 107, a later book printed under his name. His translators list it among works “unquestionably not the works of Justin”, and say it was written after the Council of Nicaea in 325.

cite.text: Answers to the Orthodox, question 107, in Migne, Patrologia Graeca, vol. 6; Dods and Reith, introduction, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1

myths.claim: “The devil is the author of all war.”
myths.truth: Not found in his works. The words that usually follow it paraphrase the *First Apology*, chapter 39. There Justin says Christians “who formerly used to murder one another” now refrain from making war on their enemies.

myths.claim: He became a Christian on “a walk along the beach at Ephesus”.
myths.truth: Justin names no town. He says only “a certain field not far from the sea”. Eusebius puts his later debate with Trypho at Ephesus, not his conversion.

cite.text: Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 3; Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 18

myths.claim: He died by drinking hemlock, like Socrates.
myths.truth: The record of his trial says he was scourged and beheaded. His translator calls the hemlock story “an absurd addition” made in some copies. His editor thinks it began among the Greeks, who gave a philosopher a philosopher's death. The verse for his day in the Greek synaxarion still says hemlock took him.

cite.text: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapter 5, and its introductory note; saint.gr

stood.lede: Each line is from his own books, in the 1885 translation.

circle.name: Priscus
circle.text: His father. Justin names him, and his grandfather Bacchius, in the first line of the *First Apology*.

circle.name: Trypho
circle.text: A Jew who had fled the war in Judea. They argued over the Scriptures for two days, and parted as friends. Eusebius calls him “a most distinguished man among the Hebrews of that day”.

cite.text: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 1 and 142; Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 18

circle.name: Crescens
circle.text: A Cynic philosopher. Eusebius says Justin often refuted him in public. Tatian says Crescens “endeavoured to inflict on Justin, and indeed on me, the punishment of death”. Eusebius's editor adds a fair warning: “we have his portrait only from the pen of his bitterest enemies.”

cite.text: Second Apology, chapter 3; Tatian, Address to the Greeks, chapter 19; Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 16, with McGiffert's notes

circle.name: Marcion
circle.text: He taught his followers to believe in another god, greater than the Creator. Justin wrote of him as “a man of Pontus, who is even at this day alive”. He also wrote a book against him, now lost.

circle.name: Tatian
circle.text: His pupil. After Justin's death he broke with the Church and condemned marriage. Irenaeus says that “as long as he continued with him he expressed no such views”.

circle.name: Euelpistus
circle.text: A servant of Caesar who died with him. Asked if Justin had made him a Christian, he said, “I willingly heard the words of Justin. But from my parents also I learned to be a Christian.”

circle.name: Irenaeus
circle.text: Bishop of Lyon a generation later. He read Justin and quotes him with approval. He saved a line from Justin's lost book against Marcion: “I would not have believed the Lord Himself, if He had announced any other than He Who is our framer, maker, and nourisher.”

death.big: He was scourged and beheaded in Rome, about 165, with six companions, for refusing to sacrifice to the gods.
paras: Rusticus, prefect of Rome, told Justin to obey the gods. He asked Justin what he taught and where the Christians met. Justin said he had tried every teaching: “I have acquiesced at last in the true doctrines, those namely of the Christians”.

Each of the others said in turn that they were Christians. Asked if Justin had made them Christians, Hierax said he always had been one. Paeon said he had it from his parents. Hierax's own parents were dead: “Christ is our true father, and faith in Him is our mother”.

Rusticus asked Justin if he supposed he would go up to heaven. “I do not suppose it,” he said, “but I know and am fully persuaded of it.” Told to sacrifice, he said, “No right-thinking person falls away from piety to impiety.”
They all refused. They were scourged and beheaded, and some believers took the bodies away in secret.

later.title: Who was behind it?
later.text: Tatian says Crescens tried to have Justin killed, and Eusebius blames him for Justin's death. The record of the trial never names him. Eusebius's editor, A. C. McGiffert, notes that Tatian's line proves only that Crescens plotted, and that “whether his plotting was successful is not stated”.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 16, with McGiffert's notes

items.q: Through prayer we can be saved on account of our Lord Jesus Christ, even when we have been punished, because this shall become to us salvation and confidence at the more fearful and universal judgment-seat of our Lord and Saviour.
items.ctx: The passage can be read another way. Lord Hailes, following the common Latin version, gave it as: “It was our chief wish to endure tortures for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so to be saved.”

items.q: Do what you will, for we are Christians, and do not sacrifice to idols.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint. Lutherans remember him too, on the same day, 1 June.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: His martyrdom was known from the first. Irenaeus mentions it in passing, as a fact everyone knew. Tertullian already calls him “philosopher and martyr”. The *Roman Martyrology* of 1916 tells it like this:

quotes.q: There suffered at Rome that remarkable man, Justin the Philosopher, who had addressed to the emperors his second Apology in defence of our religion.

extras.title: Sunday, as he described it
extras.lede: He wrote it for the emperor and for pagans. To leave it out, he says, would seem unfair. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1910 praises its “richness of detail unique for that age”.

items.title: Baptism
items.text: Those who came to believe prayed and fasted for the forgiveness of their past sins, and the church fasted with them. Then they were washed in the name of God the Father, of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit.
items.quote: Then they are brought by us where there is water, and are regenerated in the same manner in which we were ourselves regenerated.

items.title: The kiss and the cup
items.text: The newly baptised were brought to the gathering, and all prayed together. Bread and a cup of wine mixed with water were brought to the one presiding. He gave thanks at length, and all the people said Amen. Deacons gave the bread and wine to everyone, and carried some to those who were absent.
items.quote: Having ended the prayers, we salute one another with a kiss.

items.title: Not common bread
items.text: Only the baptised who lived as Christ taught could receive it. Justin says why. His translators note that the passage is “claimed alike by Calvinists, Lutherans, and Romanists”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1910 finds the Real Presence in it “with a wonderful clearness”.
items.quote: For not as common bread and common drink do we receive these; but in like manner as Jesus Christ our Saviour, having been made flesh by the Word of God, had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so likewise have we been taught that the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word, and from which our blood and flesh by transmutation are nourished, is the flesh and blood of that Jesus Who was made flesh.

items.title: On the day called Sunday
items.text: Town and country met in one place. The Gospels, which he calls the memoirs of the apostles, or the prophets were read. The one presiding preached, all rose to pray, and the bread and cup followed. Then those who had the means gave what they chose. It went to orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers.
items.quote: And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits

items.title: Why Sunday
items.text: It was the first day of creation, and the day Christ rose.
items.quote: Sunday is the day on which we all hold our common assembly, because it is the first day on which God, having wrought a change in the darkness and matter, made the world; and Jesus Christ our Saviour on the same day rose from the dead.

extras.title: Hard questions
extras.lede: Three things in his books trouble readers today. Here they are in his own words.

items.title: The Jews
items.text: The *Dialogue* is courteous, and it ends in friendship. But Justin tells Trypho that the Jews' sufferings after the war were deserved, because they killed Christ and the prophets, and cursed Christians in their synagogues. *Britannica* sums up his case: that “the gentiles have been chosen to replace Israel as God’s chosen people”. Ben Zion Bokser, in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, is blunter. He writes that Justin's “invective against Jews and Judaism entered the mainstream of Christian thought and became a sinister influence”. He ties it to the growth of Christian antisemitism.
items.quote: Accordingly, these things have happened to you in fairness and justice, for you have slain the Just One, and His prophets before Him

cite.text: Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 16; Britannica; Ben Zion Bokser, “Justin Martyr”, Encyclopaedia Judaica, 2007

items.title: The Son, second to the Father
items.text: Justin calls Christ God. He also calls Him “another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1910 credits him with the Word's “Divinity and Incarnation”. It also faults “the subordinationism of Justin's theology”, which it puts down to philosophy. He wrote long before the Council of Nicaea in 325.
items.quote: We reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third.

cite.text: First Apology, chapter 13; Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 56

items.title: A thousand years
items.text: He believed the dead would rise, and there would be a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem. He also said plainly that many good Christians disagreed with him.
items.quote: Many who belong to the pure and pious faith, and are true Christians, think otherwise.

tidbits.text: The prefect who sentenced him, Junius Rusticus, was a Stoic philosopher. He had been the favourite teacher of Marcus Aurelius, who thanks him in his *Meditations*.

He told the emperor that a statue on the Tiber honoured Simon the magician as a god. A stone dug up on the Tiber island in 1574 honours Semo Sancus, a Sabine god. Most scholars think Justin misread it.

cite.text: First Apology, chapter 26, and its note

tidbits.text: He sent the emperor to Rome's own files: the census lists made under Quirinius for Christ's birth at Bethlehem, and the Acts of Pontius Pilate for His death and healings. His editors think those Acts were lost early.
He saw the cross everywhere: in a ship's sail, a plough, the tools of diggers and craftsmen, and a man standing with his arms out. Rome's own banners, he told the emperor, carried it too.
